reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: Defined as diabetes diagnosed in the first months of life, most commonly within the first six months, when autoimmune type 1 diabetes is very unlikely
Common genetic causes include activating mutations in the KATP channel genes KCNJ11 and ABCC8 and mutations in the insulin gene INS
Presents with hyperglycaemia, poor weight gain, failure to thrive and sometimes ketoacidosis or dehydration in a young infant
KATP channel forms are frequently sulfonylurea-responsive, allowing many infants to transition from insulin to oral sulfonylurea therapy
Can be permanent or transient; transient forms often relate to chromosome 6q24 abnormalities and may relapse later in life
Some KCNJ11 mutations cause the DEND syndrome with developmental delay, epilepsy and neonatal diabetes, reflecting KATP channels in neural tissue
Urgent genetic testing is essential because the result directly changes treatment and prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: In beta cells the ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel links glucose metabolism to insulin release; rising ATP normally closes the channel, depolarising the cell and triggering secretion. Activating mutations in KCNJ11 or ABCC8 hold the channel open, preventing depolarisation and impairing insulin release, yet high-affinity sulfonylureas can close the channel independently of ATP and restore secretion. INS mutations instead cause misfolding of proinsulin and beta-cell stress, while chromosome 6q24 abnormalities perturb imprinted growth-regulating genes and typically produce transient disease.
additionalDifferentials: Type 1 diabetes mellitus presenting in infancy
Stress or illness-related transient hyperglycaemia of the newborn
Neonatal diabetes as part of a syndrome such as Wolcott-Rallison or IPEX
Iatrogenic hyperglycaemia from glucocorticoids or dextrose infusion
additionalInvestigations: Plasma glucose, ketones and blood gas to assess severity and ketoacidosis
C-peptide and insulin levels to gauge endogenous secretion
Urgent molecular genetic testing for KCNJ11, ABCC8, INS and 6q24 abnormalities
Pancreatic autoantibodies, typically negative, to help exclude autoimmune diabetes
Pancreatic imaging and syndromic assessment when structural or syndromic causes are suspected
redFlags: Diabetic ketoacidosis or severe dehydration in a young infant requiring emergency stabilisation
Neurological features such as developmental delay or seizures suggesting a DEND-type presentation
Failure to thrive or intractable hyperglycaemia needing rapid diagnostic clarification
Associated syndromic features indicating a broader multisystem disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies by genotype: many KATP channel cases achieve excellent control on sulfonylureas with potential neurodevelopmental benefit, transient forms may remit though relapse is common, while syndromic and INS-related forms carry a more guarded outlook.
pitfalls: Assuming any infantile diabetes is type 1 and committing to lifelong insulin without genetic testing
Missing the opportunity to transition sulfonylurea-responsive cases off insulin
Overlooking neurodevelopmental features that indicate a KATP channel syndrome
Failing to plan follow-up for transient neonatal diabetes that can relapse in later life
management: Start insulin to control hyperglycaemia at presentation and to treat any ketoacidosis or dehydration
After urgent genotyping, trial an oral sulfonylurea in KATP-channel (KCNJ11/ABCC8) disease to close the channel and transition many infants off insulin
Maintain insulin therapy for INS-gene, 6q24 and sulfonylurea-unresponsive forms
Monitor glycaemic control, feeding and growth, and screen for the neurodevelopmental features of DEND syndrome in KCNJ11 disease
Anticipate remission in transient (6q24) forms and follow up for later relapse in childhood or adolescence
Refer to paediatric endocrinology and clinical genetics, with genetic counselling for the family
